pages.text: Colours Day had arrived, and the school field was a riot of colour. Red House, Blue House, Green House and Yellow House stood in four blocks, waving flags and banging drums. Derrick, the captain of Red House, looked at the scoreboard from last year. Red was last. Again. “Six years without a trophy,” he groaned. “We need more than luck.”
sentences: Colours Day had arrived, and the school field was a riot of colour.
Red House, Blue House, Green House and Yellow House stood in four blocks, waving flags and banging drums.
Derrick, the captain of Red House, looked at the scoreboard from last year.
Red was last.
Again.
“Six years without a trophy,” he groaned.
“We need more than luck.”
pages.alt: A school field with four coloured house teams waving flags, and a boy captain looking at a scoreboard.

pages.text: Coach Bartels handed Derrick a clipboard. “A captain’s first job is not to run fastest,” he said. “It is to find where each person fits.” Derrick thought about that. He held a meeting after school. “Everyone has a place,” he said. “Runners, jumpers, throwers, cheerleaders, timekeepers, drummers, first-aiders. Even the person who carries the water bottles matters.”

pages.text: Adjoa raised a shy hand. “I am not fast,” she said. “But I never get tired. My legs just keep going.” Coach Bartels clapped. “You are a long-distance runner,” he said. “That is a talent, and there are points for the fifteen hundred metres.” Adjoa smiled for the first time in weeks. For two weeks, the team trained before school, shared water and cheered each other on.

pages.alt: A girl with a stopwatch smiles as a coach points to a long-distance track marking.

pages.text: On the day, Red House won the relay by a whisker, lost the high jump, and came second in the tug of war. In the final race, the fifteen hundred metres, Adjoa ran steadily at the back of the pack. At the last lap, she passed one runner, then another. The crowd roared. Adjoa crossed the line in second place, and Red House shrieked with joy.

pages.alt: A girl runner in a red vest overtakes others on the final lap of a track while a crowd cheers.

pages.text: Then came the shock. Blue House won overall by two points. Derrick’s heart sank. Some of the Red House students booed. “Stop,” said Derrick, raising his hand. “We came in second. That is the best we have done in six years. Congratulate Blue House.” He walked over and shook the Blue captain’s hand. “Well played,” he said. “See you next year.”

pages.text: Coach Bartels pulled Derrick aside. “That was real sportsmanship,” he said. “Anyone can be gracious when they win. A true captain is gracious when they lose.” Derrick nodded. “We trained together, we cheered each other, we played fair,” he said. “That matters more than the trophy.” Then he grinned. “But I still want the trophy next year.”

pages.text: That night, Derrick wrote to his friend Prosper, who had moved to another school. His address and the date came first. “Plot 21, Ridge Road, Tema. 19th February, 2027. Dear Prosper, I hope you are well. You will not believe what happened on Colours Day. Red House came second overall, and our newest runner, Adjoa, finished the fifteen hundred metres in second place. We did not win the trophy, but we have never been prouder. How was your sports day? Write back soon. Your friend, Derrick.”

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: Derrick described the event in complete sentences with specific details such as who, what and where. He did not write “OMG”, “lol” or “we were gonna win”. Instead, he wrote “you will not believe what happened” and “we have never been prouder”. Excited feelings can be shown with strong, full words. The end.
